So, you’ve read my introduction, and you’ve decided you’re interested. Good! There’s a LOT of obstacles standing in your way, but once you hurdle those, you’ll find that it becomes easier in time.

I thought that securing financing is probably the first thing we should talk about. After all, no money, no rentals. :)

In the housing bubble from the mid 2000’s, almost anyone could get a loan from a bank for a house. People who made crappy money, had poor credit history, etc, were given loans who otherwise normally wouldn’t get them. This obviously could go on for so long, before it imploded.

When the market dropped, banks tightened up their lending rules, and getting a loan became harder. Now there’s a few things you’ll need to understand. When I talk about a loan, I mean a commercial loan, vs. a consumer loan that you would normally get when you buy your house you live in. There is a distinction there, and I want to be clear on what I mean. What’s the main differences between the two? In a consumer loan, you can get away with putting down as little as 3% for a down payment. This means $6,000 for a $200,000 piece of property. Your loan would be for 30 years, and would have other stipulations attached to it.

In a commercial loan, you must have at LEAST 20% down, and certain banks like to see 25% down. So, on that same $200,000 piece of property, you’re looking at between $40,000-$50,000 for a down payment. In cash. That means no putting it on your credit card, or leveraging other sources towards the down payment. The loan also is for 20 years instead of 30, and and bank wants to see at least 6 months worth of reserves in your account.

So, in the above example, if a bank required 25% down, and 6 months worth of reserves at 5% interest over 20 years (I’m using round numbers to make it easy, yours may vary), you would need at LEAST $55,934 in cash. ($50,000 for down payment and $989 monthly payment x 6 months).

You can see why it seems almost impossible for people to get into real estate investing. Staring down the barrel of needing almost $56k in cash when you’re making $50k a year seems like it’ll never happen.

But it can, and I’ll tell you how in my next article.

But first, let’s also take a minute to talk about your credit rating. When you buy your first place, you have almost no business credit, but you have your personal credit This is CRITICAL to have as high as possible. When I was married to my ex, we would do our bills here and there. We had the money for it, but we didn’t really put much thought into paying the bills exactly on time. This crippled our credit score. When I divorced, I didn’t want to deal with paying the bills all the time, so I put all my bills on autopay and set my work paycheck to be direct deposited. That way I didn’t have to think about paying bills. They were automatically taken care of for me, and all I had to do was show up at work and go about my day. My credit score skyrocketed accordingly.

To give you an idea, when I bought my car about a year ago, my credit score was 818. Perfect score is 850. It took me a long while to get there, but it is worth it to see the bank manager’s eyes light up when they pull your credit report and know that they can approve the deal you want to make.

Now, I’m not making a super high amount of money in my current job, but my credit score reflects that I am highly responsible with money and pay my bills on time. That means the world to the bank, and it will make it much easier for them to approve your loans.

Also, get rid of credit card debt if you can. Don’t max out your credit cards, or close out of accounts that are paid off. If you have 5 cards with 10k available on them, you have 50k in available credit. So even if one of those cards has 9k on it, you’re still in much better position than if you only had 1 card with the 9k on it. (roughly 20% maxed out on 5 cards vs. 90% maxed out on 1 card)

So, you’ve managed to get your credit score up high enough to where a bank will loan you money. So, let’s pick a place and crunch some numbers shall we? I’m going to give you a hard rule about real estate investing:

Always make a profit. Sounds simple right?

ALWAYS MAKE A PROFIT.

I have seen people buy $300,000 houses while barely breaking even, banking on the idea that the appreciation of the house will make them rich. Houses don’t always appreciate, and can even go DOWN in value. Just look at what happened when the housing bubble popped.

Now, you’ll need to understand that I did a ton of research and made a bunch of phone calls before I ended up with this particular property. I’d find another property, and someone would have already snatched it up. You may be thinking “Wait, you were talking about $200k pieces of property, and this one is only $40k. WTF”?

You’re right. I was looking at properties in my general area, but they were WAY too expensive. I was looking at properties that when it was all said and done, I’d be making about 4% on my money. "Not bad in this economy" I’m hearing you all say. But in my first rental, I pulled in almost 12% after it was all said and done.

Now, for some real world numbers on that first rental:

Purchase price: $110,000 (Listed for $139,900, and was bought by the owner for $200,000 during the bubble for context) Down payment: $22,000 Monthly payment with taxes: $649 Paint, fixing misc issues, etc: $3,000 Total out of pocket: $25,000 Rent: $995 Management company: $99.50 (10% of gross rent) Total: $995.00-$99.50-$649= $246.50 $25,000/($246.50*12 months) = 11.83%

Pretty nice right? There is literally NO reason why you can’t do the same.

What I did with the profit was sock it into a savings account and had the mortgage taken out of the same account automatically. The management company (which I will do a separate article on), is worth it’s weight in gold. Unless you like getting phone calls at 3am, excuses as to why the rent is late, etc, get a management company. I can’t recommend one enough.

What does that mean? That means that my tenant pays the mortgage down, the management company, AND puts almost $250 a month in my pocket. That’s what I mean when I say always make a profit. I’ll also go into what to do when lease renewal time comes around and what to do when something goes wrong (I’ve had those all happen with me in my first rental, and my responses has made my tenant more happy to stay right where he’s at)

Also, I have a pretty neat spreadsheet I'd be willing to post to help you all out!

Now that you've gotten this far, if you have any questions, feel free to ask away!

This is actually really poor advice and here's why:

In many states, when you sign a contract with the DLD to get your license, there is a clause along the lines that you will submit to a breathalyzer test upon suspicion of a DUI. If you get pulled over and refuse to submit to a test, you violate this contract and that alone is grounds for arrest.

Once arrested, they'll take you to a station and draw blood, etc. However, once you go to trial, you'll have 2 (or more) things against you: Driving under the influence (criminal offense) AND refusal to submit to a test (civil offense). Both are handled separately. In most states, breaking your contract with the DLD results in a mandatory suspension of your license for well over a year. In Utah, the minimum is 18 months. Had you submitted to the test, you could possible get your license back in 120 days (again, Utah law).
